new_statements.quote: Nganasan has both primary and secondary stress. Correlates of stress in Nganasan are fundamental frequency, duration and amplitude. Normally, primary stress is assigned to the final syllable if it is heavy (CVV), and to antepenultimate syllable if the final is light [...] It appears, therefore, that while primary stress assignment is concerned with the right edge of a word, in that it is the penultimate mora that gets stressed (except situations where either schwa or [ï] is penultimate), secondary stress is assigned 'from the left': aside from CV.CVV-initial words and clash restrictions, secondary stress is placed on the odd-numbered moras of a word. [...] stress is never on the last syllable.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: File (295 pp., MIT DSpace hdl 1721.1/47830, open) opened with extracted text; printed page numbers = PDF page numbers. p. 23, section 2.2.1.1 'Basic Facts', reads exactly: 'Nganasan has both primary and secondary stress. Correlates of stress in Nganasan are fundamental frequency, duration and amplitude. Normally, primary stress is assigned to the final syllable if it is heavy (CVV), and to antepenultimate syllable if the final is light:' followed by data (4) bakúnu 'salmon' / bàkunú-mə, tïrími, káDar / kaDár-mə, kümaá, birí-ə, lehuá; p. 24: 'It appears, therefore, that while primary stress assignment is concerned with the right edge of a word, in that it is the penultimate mora that gets st…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the penultimate vocalic mora of the word: on a final syllable with a long vowel/vowel sequence (kümaá 'knife', lehuá 'board'), otherwise on the penultimate syllable (bakúnu 'salmon', káDar 'light', bakunú-mə 'my salmon'); the p. 23 word 'antepenultimate' is contradicted by the author's own data (4) and by her p. 24 summary and reads as a slip for 'penultimate'. Stress is computed over the whole inflected word and is never word-final on a light syllable. When the penultimate vowel is ə or ï, stress shifts (obligatorily or optionally) to a neighbouring more sonorous vowel (section 2.2.1.2).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Secondary stress is left-aligned, on odd-numbered moras counting from the word beginning (bàkunù-mənú-mə), except that a word-initial CV.CVV sequence puts the secondary stress on the CVV syllable, and clash is avoided.
new_statements.exceptions: Hedge 'Normally'; sonority-driven retraction/advancement when penultimate (and/or antepenultimate) vowel is ə or ï (no shift off a, e, o, u, i, ü in the Avam variety she recorded; de Lacy's data also show shifts from u, i, fn. 3); adjacent vowels never both stressed. Note the older account in Tereshchenko 1993 p. 351 (downloaded) differs: first-syllable stress in disyllables unless a long vowel/diphthong attracts it, additional stress on the 3rd (rarely 5th) syllable, stress usually retained on the root under affixation.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress on inflected word forms (citation forms and possessive/prolative suffixed forms elicited in fieldwork, Avam dialect); derived/suffixed words 'are evaluated as a whole for the purposes of stress assignment' (p. 23).
new_statements.identity_note: Both quoted sources describe the Avam (western/central) dialect of Nganasan: Vaysman 2009 p. 22 'The data presented in this chapter is from the Avam dialect'; Tereshchenko 1993 p. 350 'Очерк написан на материале речи авамских нганасанов'. Glottolog treats Avam and Vadey as dialects under ngan1291; the statement is catalogued at language level ngan1291.

sources.note: Primary and secondary stress; correlates F0, duration, amplitude. Primary stress on the penultimate mora (final syllable if CVV, otherwise the penult; p. 23 prose says 'antepenultimate' but data (4) bakúnu, tïrími, káDar and the p. 24 summary show penult), with obligatory/optional shifts off penultimate ə and ï (section 2.2.1.2); secondary stress left-aligned on odd-numbered moras; stress never on the last syllable; suffixed words re-evaluated as wholes (bakúnu > bakunú-mə).

sources.quote: P5. Stress type. Values: Stress is distinctive and has a fixed position [F] / Stress is distinctive and has a variable position [V] / Stress is not distinctive [N]. This system of stress types has been described by Rozhanskiy (2013). In many cases, the choice of the value for a particular language can be controversial because there are no good prosodic descriptions for most Uralic languages and the information given in grammars is often contradictory. [pp. 17-18] ... Table 1. Phonetic and phonological features of Uralic languages ... Samoyedic P1 P2 P3 P4 P5 P6 P7 / Nganasan 2 + + 0 V -/+ + [p. 19]
sources.locator: printed pp. 17-19: feature P5 'Stress type' defined pp. 17-18; Table 1, Samoyedic block, Nganasan row, p. 19, column P5 = V
sources.note: Coarse typological value only: Nganasan is coded P5 = V, 'stress is distinctive and has a variable position' (not fixed, not non-distinctive; no mixed mark such as V(N)). No stress rule, no weight statement, no secondary-stress or domain statement, and no tone statement is given; the survey does not name the grammar used for Nganasan. Compatible with the catalog's weight-sensitive coding (stress position varies), but it neither states nor tests the CVV-final rule. The authors themselves warn that P5 values 'can be controversial' for lack of prosodic descriptions.

sources.quote: § 9. Основными правилами, определяющими ударение того или иного слога в слове, для нганасанского диалекта можно считать следующие: 1. В двусложных словах, содержащих краткие гласные, или односложных словах, содержащих дифтонг, состоящий из кратких гласных, главное ударение падает на первый слог (или первый компонент дифтонга), напр.: tomu ‘мышь’, samu ‘шапка’, nua ‘сын’, kua ‘береза’. 2. То же правило распространяется на слова, содержащие в первом слоге долгий гласный или дифтонг, напр.: tadaj ‘ключица’, faemu ‘меховая обувь’. 3. В двусложных словах, содержащих в первом слоге краткий гласный, а во втором долгий, а также односложных словах, содержащих дифтонг, вторым компонентом которого является долгий гласный, главное ударение падает на второй слог (или второй компонент дифтонга), напр.: куша ‘нож’, fear) ‘ладонь’. 4. В многосложных словах дополнительное ударение обычно располагается через один слог от слога, несущего главное ударение, причем слог, содержащий долгий гласный или дифтонг, считается за два слога, содержащих краткие гласные, напр.: kua ‘береза’, местн. п. ед. ч.— kuatanu; lu ‘одежда’, местн. п. ед. ч.— lutanu; peta ‘котел’, им. п. мн. ч. 1-го л. ед. ч.— petaina. В ряд
sources.note: Confirms the catalog's weight-sensitive coding: main stress is initial in disyllables unless the second syllable holds a long vowel or diphthong, in which case it falls on the second (final) syllable; long vowels and diphthongs count as heavy (two short syllables) for secondary-stress placement. Secondary stress stated: normally every other syllable from the main stress on a mora count, with an exception where it falls two syllables away (fatamandatum). Prokof'ev says nothing about closed syllables, so the catalog's 'closed syllables are light' (Vaysman) is neither confirmed nor contradicted.

sources.citation: de Lacy, Paul. 2004. Markedness conflation in Optimality Theory. Phonology 21(2): 145-199. doi:10.1017/S0952675704000193
sources.quote: Putting the influence of vowel sonority aside momentarily, Nganasan has a fairly standard right-aligned trochaic stress pattern. Helimski (1998: 486) describes stress as falling on a final CVV syllable, and otherwise the penult, as illustrated in (11). Stress domains consist of a root and certain affixes; secondary stress falls on heavy syllables and every other light syllable preceding a stress (i.e. it is quantity-sensitive, trochaic and right-edge oriented [...]). Syllables with long vowels (CV:) are heavy, CVC and CV syllables are light. Stressed vowels are realised with longer duration and loudness than unstressed vowels (see §3.6.3 for details). [...] However, in trisyllabic words where all syllables are light (i.e. CV or CVC), stress can optionally fall on the antepenultimate syllable if it contains a non-high peripheral vowel [a e o] and the penult is a light syllable with a central or high peripheral vowel [i y u ə ɨ] (Helimski 1998: 486).

Ez a szabály opcionálisan megsérthető, ha nyílt szótagban a szótag magja felső nyelvállású magánhangzó vagy ə. Ilyenkor a főhangsúly áttolódhat az előző szótagra: ba'rusi ~ 'barusi 'gonosz lény'. A diftongusok magukra vonják a hangsúlyt: horaS'aj 'falevél'. [secondary stress, same section:] Egy-egy ritmikai egység két szótagot ölel föl, az utolsó, maradék egységben állhat három szótag is. Egy ritmikai egységben csak egy hangsúly lehet, tehát, ha az utolsó egységben már van főhangsúly (') valamelyik szótagon, nem lehet mellékhangsúlyos az adott egység első szótagja is. sources.note: Hungarian-language chrestomathy; the phonology chapter (HANGTAN) is by Várnai Zsuzsa. Main stress: generally penultimate (not initial as in most Uralic); optionally shifts one syllable left when the penult is open with a high vowel or ə (ba'rusi ~ 'barusi); diphthongs attract stress (horaS'aj 'leaf', final). sources.note: A word-formation monograph (denominal and deverbal verbal suffixes, nominal derivation, suffix sequences). No phonology chapter; the words Betonung, Akzent, Wortakzent, Intonation and Ton (as prosody) do not occur anywhere in the text. The only prosodic content is passing use of the mora-counting rhythmic consonant gradation (rhythmischer Stufenwechsel: weak grade in odd-numbered moras, p. 126; the suffix -NTƏ altered by rhythmic and syllabic gradation and nunnation, p. 61), for whose rules the author refers to Helimski 1994, 1998.
